claim: The core library is the product; the CLI is an add-on.
why: The product is the protocol, its vectors and one implementation. Other languages meet it at the JSON format, the CLI or a socket. Lean on existing standards wherever one fits.

claim: Rust, in a new strange-loops repo.
why: Historical plan: a core crate, a CLI crate, and adjacent Lean model, vectors and scenarios enforce budgets. Version 31 chose Rust for phones and browser extensions. Version 35 removed the Go core (PR 6) while model boundaries were reviewed. Rust is now implemented in rust/, with a pure core and a fixture evaluator. JS and Rust check all protocol fixture families and external standards. The loops CLI and its storage over .loops/ are built (step 2, closed on 2026-11-20); budget tooling remains planned. The proposed .loops/ migration remains a collector in the old repo.

claim: One word per concept, one concept per word.
why: The Glossary lists the vocabulary. Record replaces fact. Anchor, thing, place and realm absorb genesis, subject, residence and topology. Seal retires: observers emit, vertices tick and ticks cover records. Normative prose lives in the protocol. LatestBy replaces Upsert. Vertex stays: it is where loops meet.

claim: R1: Byte text uses canonical lower-case unpadded base32hex.
why: The alphabet follows ASCII order. Canonical id text and digest bytes have the same order. Readers refuse wrong lengths and nonzero pad bits.

claim: R2: The id preimage is the JCS object containing commit and env.
why: The object defines the preimage. It is not a byte concatenation.

claim: R3: Signed bytes are the version prefix followed by the id text in UTF-8.
why: The prefix is loops/record/v1:. It separates the signed record id from other messages.

claim: R4: Each instant has one canonical UTC spelling.
why: The writer uses Z and seconds 00 through 59. An optional fraction has 1 to 9 digits and ends in a nonzero digit. Date precision remains part of the claim.

claim: R5: Typed references use a lower-case prefix, and sets sort by UTF-16 code units.
why: References use prefix:value. Set normalization also removes repeats and omits empty sets, except sets, where an empty set is written as []: absent and empty differ there.

claim: R6: Unknown envelope fields receive a named refusal first.
why: The reader checks keys before values. It returns envelope-field-unknown before kind-empty. Variation belongs in the payload.

claim: D2: Text is Unicode scalar values; a lone surrogate is refused by name before hashing.
why: The refusal is string-not-unicode. It covers values, member names, envelope fields and what a batch holds, in text and in direct-value APIs. It follows envelope-field-unknown and precedes kind-empty. A payload text gets it only when the text is JSON by its syntax. Nothing is substituted, U+FFFD included.

claim: D3: A number past binary64's range is refused by the writer's number check.
why: The refusal is the existing number-out-of-range, last in the writer's order. The core's number type stays finite. An input adapter carries the overflow to that check and to the spec parser; it refuses neither earlier nor under another name. A reader's own records must hold finite numbers.

claim: A store is a set, not a sequence.
why: Receipt order leaves the fold. Underneath: immutable single-writer segments, content-addressed blobs, a derived index.

claim: Every record has an observer, and two times.
why: Ingestion is a dumb observer reporting what a source holds: hearsay. emitted is the writer's word (RFC 3339); occurred is an optional claimed span that can be coarse.

claim: occurred is a span with a closed grammar: dates, instants and intervals, never a duration.
why: Each occurred value names one span. Content order reads that span; future windows use its start. Calendar dates are UTC days. EDTF Level 1 qualifiers (2009~) and trailing unspecified digits (201X) retain one span. Qualifiers never change it. Intervals join two points and may have an open end (2019/..). Spans order by start, then end, with open ends last. Content order compares span, emitted, then id digest bytes, never spellings. Without occurred, a record has its emitted instant span. Canonical base32hex id text has the same order as digest bytes. Durations repeat what an end instant says. Seasons, open or unknown starts, unknown ends and years past 9999 fail with occurred-not-span. Accepting less would invalidate stored records. Version 35.

claim: Identity is a content hash; signatures sit beside it.
why: A salted payload commitment, an id over the canonical {commit, env}, an Ed25519 signature over loops/record/v1: plus the id. References stay opaque. Records are signed by default and a store carries its writers' key bindings, so it verifies itself. The version in the signed prefix lets a reader refuse only what is newer than it knows.

claim: Writing the same record twice is a no-op.
why: A record's id covers its envelope, including emitted, plus its salt and payload. The same draft written twice is the same record, and set union absorbs it, in a batch or across batches. A new observation gets a fresh salt, so it gets a new id and is simply a new record. Version 35.

claim: A record erases through its envelope field erases; any kind may erase.
why: erases is a set of record ids, refused unless each is one, and never a label. It sits on the envelope, so every reader applies it, whatever its grant. Targets in about were rejected: a kind would decide which reading of about applied. No kind is reserved for erasing, so the field carries the meaning by itself, and a revision can erase what it replaces: prev: [r:X], erases: [r:X]. Authority keys on the field. Version 35.

claim: A field belongs on the envelope only if the core reads it.
why: The envelope holds kind, observer, emitted, optional occurred, about, of, prev, under, erases and sets. derived-from, seen and refs belong in payloads. Readers refuse unknown envelope fields.

claim: A payload is here, withheld or erased; supersession reads only the envelope.
why: prev sits on the envelope. Withholding or erasing payloads preserves each thing's head ids. A record superseded within a thing cannot become current there. A payload test answers unknown when its payload is unavailable. Results count covered records they cannot read. Added in version 32.

claim: Erasure is per store and small; privacy is withholding, not hiding.
why: Erasure removes payloads but keeps commitments and ids. Consistent forms determine one settled record per id, independent of read order. A reader keeps a held payload unless a held eraser names its id. A bare erased copy cannot suppress a held payload. Disclosure splits by kind when recording. Planned disclosure keeps derived data under its least-public input's grant.

claim: Writers bound every number’s magnitude; numeric readers additionally require whole values.
why: RFC 8785 reads numbers as binary64 before canonicalization. The final 13:25 human ruling keeps Option A: writers refuse any magnitude above 253−1, whole or not (number-out-of-range); 1e30 is refused. Within-range fractions are accepted. Numeric readers additionally require whole values. Exact decimal or large-integer values belong in strings.

claim: One checked write path, and what it returns carries the proof.
why: write checks the envelope, salt length, repeated members at any depth, then nonfinite numbers or any number outside ±(253−1), whole or not. Within-range fractions pass. A batch uses the same path, with refusal priority independent of draft order and prev order. It returns a Written record carrying the proof, including distinct member names. Version 35 (PR 7), with the final 13:25 writer-range ruling.

claim: A fold reads a payload by one stated rule, and no field name is special.
why: A held payload that is an object supplies its top-level members as fields; any other value supplies none. present means the member was written, also when it holds null, {}, [] or "". A list reads as a set of its members under is, not and by, and is never a number. Nothing reads inside a nested object. value and n were once on every record, as empty text and 0; they are now fields like any other, so a record without n is unread to a sum of n. Ruled on 2026-11-21 (payload values, seven choices) and stated in the model as payload.read. Version 36.

claim: Observers are things, with lineages under their names.
why: A lineage id is the hash of its anchor. Names, keys and models are records about a lineage. Names never take part in matching: they resolve at read, through name tables and @home.

claim: Naming, key binding and authority stay separate.
why: Authority is a grant record, pointed to by under. One stance shape covers affirm, adopt, dispute, retire and authorize. A delegate is a shared seat; an identity that emerges starts its own lineage and adopts what it wants to own.

claim: A label may stand in under.
why: A changeset can create grant @g and act under it. under accepts labels, like about, of and prev, and participates in cycle detection. A writer refuses an under target it doesn't hold, in the batch or the store (under-unknown; Kyle, 2026-11-13). Whether the target is a grant, and whether it authorizes the act, is for future standing checks. A label grants no extra authority. Version 35.

claim: Keys in tiers, and presence for what takes effect.
why: A lineage pins its root key. The standing plan gives each device presence and emit keys; agents receive session keys. Effective authority changes require a person present. A grant records presence ahead of time: agents propose and narrow, never widen. Standing ends by retirement through held records, never by time.

claim: D8a: A record is an emit of one thing, named in its envelope by of.
why: of is one typed reference, a record id or a natural key, read as written and never resolved through another record. Only a root leaves it out; a record with prev states it (of-missing). latest-by, per-thing state and heads run over it, and every prev target is of the same thing. A writer refuses an of naming a held record that is not a root (of-not-root). A record without of keeps its bytes and id. Kyle, 2026-11-10; built in the model, the vectors, JavaScript and Rust. The refusal names and their order are an implementer's choice, not yet confirmed.

claim: D8b: about only mentions; it never makes a head.
why: where and collect still read it, so everything said about a thing stays a fold. from.about is a mention test and from.of takes a thing's records. A link that many writers add to and remove is a thing of its own whose about names both ends (the edges ruling below). Kyle, 2026-11-10; built with D8a. D8c, keys a record declares it sets, is ruled and built: its envelope field sets, every fold type following keys, and the keyed slice laws.

claim: Identity lives in the record, in of.
why: A thing uses a root record id or a typed natural key computed by tooling, such as a URL or code birth key. The core compares those references. Observers and stores use proposed reserved *-anchor kinds. A vertex instead hashes its canonical spec and parameters; it has no anchor or standing. Proposed equivalence, provenance and succession remain separate; resolve-by joins identities at read. Unknown names follow the planned store maturity rules.

claim: A facet is one kind of one thing, emitted whole.
why: Current state is LatestBy per thing; from then chooses kinds. Since D8c (below) a thing's fields are read key by key from the keys each record declares, so an update no longer has to restate the whole; a facet read by kind remains a proposal. prev is a set, so forks retain several heads. Links are new records, never edits to about. A record is of exactly one thing: the one of names, or without of its own id. A root, with no of and no prev, starts a thing named by its id; its revision states that id in of, so unrelated roots never fork each other. Version 35; restated by D8a.

claim: prev is succession within a thing.
why: Within a fixed admitted set, succession affects only its own thing. Writers refuse unheld prev targets outside the batch (prev-unknown), an of naming a held record that is not a root (of-not-root), and targets of another thing (prev-unrelated). Readers reject held targets of another thing, but admit unknown targets because they cannot judge them. Planned moving or narrowing uses explicit retire records. Replacement rules read only envelopes; future standing supplies authority. Version 34; restated by D8a.

claim: D8c: a record declares the keys it sets, and a keyed thing is read key by key.
why: The envelope field sets names the top-level payload keys a record sets; without it the record is read whole. A slot that follows keys reads each key from its live setters: the records that set it and that no later setter of it replaced. So an emit of status alone no longer drops title. Two live setters that disagree show as a conflict, and the core picks no winner. The envelope of a keyed thing is read from its heads. Ruled on 2026-11-13 and 2026-11-14, and built in the model and both implementations. Version 36.

claim: A writer's tool names every live record of the thing it writes.
why: When every emit names every live record under it, the live records of a thing, read alone, give its whole keyed state (keyed.anchored), so a reader can hold a slice and not the history. loops emit fills this in. It also copies the heads' about and, since 2026-11-21, their occurred when they agree: an update to a thing that occurred in 2009 stays in 2009 unless its writer states a new occurrence. The protocol infers none of it: each is written into the envelope at write time, and a changeset (emit -) states its own, unless it asks for the same filling with --fill. Version 36.

claim: Edges need no change to the envelope.
why: Three classes. A reference with one value is a scalar payload field, and two writers who disagree on it are a real conflict. A set that one observer asserts whole is a payload list, read as a set. An open edge that many writers add to and remove from is one thing per edge: a record of its own whose payload holds rel, from, to and state, and whose about mentions both ends. Labelled about was rejected: it would fork on two concurrent adds and still could not hold an edge's attributes. Ruled on 2026-11-21. Version 36.

claim: A vertex is a question; a store is a thing you write into.
why: A vertex owns no storage or sources. Its id hashes its canonical spec and parameters; a name record points to the current id. It has no anchor, key or standing. Equal specs and parameters name the same vertex wherever evaluated (version 32). The store plan uses lineage declarations and machine-local places. Dated declarations accrete without migrations; admission enforces maturity.

claim: Specs are JSON, stored as records.
why: protocol/spec.md is normative; protocol/schema.md and JSON Schema files do not exist. Today a spec is a file, .loops/vertices/<name>.json. The storage plan uses vertex records and note comments. Parameterized templates remain proposed. The core accepts supported specs as data. Every accepted spec has at least one source; absent or empty from fails with from-missing.

claim: Six folds in two families, plus modifiers.
why: Count, Sum, Min, Max, LatestBy and Collect form the supported fold vocabulary. Supported modifiers follow protocol/spec.md. by groups count, sum, min, max and collect by an envelope field, a typed-reference prefix of about (env.about:<prefix>) or a payload field. Historical proposals include order, set mode, windows and ranking-only weight-by; they are not implemented grammar. The proposed Avg lens divides Sum by Count. With each input id supplied once, commuting accumulators and over-head folds obey their set laws. Incremental over-head evaluation needs cached LatestBy state, not merely a cached answer. Max's scalar state cannot track changing heads; this proves no impossibility for all bounded-state algorithms. The Rust sum is unbounded. The JavaScript sum is exact to a signed 128-bit total; that limit was found on 2026-11-21 and is on the roadmap to remove or state. Future bounded ports must refuse overflow. Version 32.

claim: Predicates are a closed, typed set.
why: Six where operators test individual records. Future boundaries can test vertex state. No regex, arithmetic, user code or effects: an observer records classifications instead. Proposed collectors own parse pipelines; future boundaries omit run hooks.

claim: where can test any envelope field, named explicitly.
why: Envelope tests use env.kind, env.observer, env.emitted, env.occurred, env.about, env.of, env.prev, env.under and env.erases. Bare names identify payload fields. Unknown env. names are refused. Arguments must fit their fields: typed references, record ids, times, or supported payload scalars. Numeric tests require safe whole values after binary64 ingestion. Numeric complement laws additionally require a numeric bound. Missing and nonwhole values need not pass either bound. Time equality compares spans, not spelling; time bounds compare starts. Envelope tests select after supersession. A record without occurred passes neither time bound. A window instead uses its emitted. Windows include starts at their lower bound and exclude starts at their upper bound. Ruled on 2026-11-20: a window is a where on that time, applied after the heads (under Resolution, below); it is not built. Filtering before supersession could revive replaced records. Whole-span bounds were rejected: January ends before its year despite their equal starts. Observer tests use lineage ids until name tables arrive. Specs refuse repeated keys and empty where maps. Latest-by always writes follow: "prev" or "keys". Version 35.

claim: unread counts what couldn't be read.
why: A covered record is unread when its payload test is unknown or its selected numeric fold cannot read a safe whole field. Count each id once per slot, or each unread thing once for a slot that follows keys. Collect counts unknown candidates before its limit. Full-result equality needs answering tests and fold-readable covered records. Historical version 35 counted only uncertainty affecting the limit and overclaimed unread: 0. PR 13 removed those claims. A stronger limit-sensitive guarantee remains future work, not a current theorem.

claim: Supersession runs over everything held; selection comes after.
why: Each thing's state uses its records from the fixed admitted set, before vertex selection. from, envelope tests and payload tests then choose among heads. Selecting first could revive a record superseded by another kind, an excluded source, a failed filter or a withheld successor. Without follow, count and sum include selected history, even when superseded; following prev they read the heads, and following keys the things. Found while modelling the spec (versions 33 and 34).

claim: A tick is a value; a stored tick is a signed record.
why: Future tick design: a content tick hashes its vertex, covered ids and result. Machines with the same inputs can recompute that id. Persistence uses an ordinary tick record signed by its writer, preserving one envelope. A witness tick records the runner's observed set. Erased numeric inputs leave only the signature as evidence for prior results. Proposed revisits create ticks citing earlier ticks. These transitions are not implemented proofs. Version 32.

claim: Every result has two names.
why: Results have an input key and a result hash. The result hash is built (res:, below). The input key is ruled in part, in that it names which covered records were read open, and is not built. Downstream keys use result hashes, so unchanged results stop work. Incremental commuting folds need accumulator state; over-head folds need LatestBy state. Cached result values alone are insufficient.

claim: State references form a DAG; ticks may loop.
why: Future state references form an acyclic dependency graph. Tick feedback crosses explicit recorded steps. Hygiene vertices would expose drift and self-reinforcing salience. Reference, boundary and tick transitions still need models and proofs.

claim: A result has canonical bytes, and a hash of its own spelled res:.
why: The codec writes every slot of a vertex's result as one JCS object. An integer is decimal text, so a sum past 253 keeps every digit. A listed record is its id alone, without what the reader holds of it, so a reader who holds a payload and one who had it erased write the same bytes wherever they list the same ids. No tag is needed: position alone tells an integer from text. The hash is res: and base32hex of SHA-256 over a versioned label and those bytes; it cannot be a record's commitment, which is h:. Ruled on 2026-11-11, 2026-11-20 and 2026-11-21; built, with vectors. Version 36.

claim: A cut is a part closed downward, and "as of T" is everything the records emitted by T build on.
why: emitted is the writer's claim, so a record can build on one with a later emitted. The records emitted by T can then hold a record without what it was written on, and read a state no holder could have read: 96 of 3,504 cuts did, with clocks an hour apart. A part closed downward over prev is a state the store could have been in. "As of T" takes the records emitted by T and everything they reach through prev. It changes no record, no writer and no refusal. Ruled on 2026-11-20; the laws are keyed.cut and cut.prefix. Version 36.

claim: A content tick folds a set named outright, and says which covered records it read open.
why: covers lists ids. emitted is one way to choose them and never a parameter of a fold, so no fold changed. What a store held at a time is not a fold's parameter either: nothing in a record says when it arrived, so only a witness tick taken then can answer. A holder before an erasure and one after it compute different results for the same ids wherever a value reads a payload, so a tick's inputs name which covered records were read open, and one set of inputs never names two results. Ruled on 2026-11-20. Version 36.

claim: A window is a where, applied after the heads.
why: A window tests the time content order already uses: a record's occurred when it states one, its emitted when it does not. Taking the window first, then folding, showed as current a record that a revision had moved out of the window in 428 of 660 trials. So a window is not a second mechanism beside where. Ruled on 2026-11-20. The field is env.when (ruled 2026-11-21); it is in the model with its laws, and Rust is being built. Version 36.

claim: The tick record is an ordinary record whose payload is the whole tick.
why: Ruled on 2026-11-21 (the tick record note). It is built: the model with its laws and vectors, Rust, and the verbs loops tick and loops tick --check; a tick written on one machine checks the same on a second (2026-11-21). The payload holds the spec and its hash, the version of the rules, covers, the covered records read without a payload, and the result with its hash. A tick among the covered records is one record, never opened up. A store admits a tick without checking it; a verb checks, and answers same, differs or cannot check. This replaces "a content tick hashes its vertex, covered ids and result" above: a tick has no id but its record id. Version 36.

claim: A place is a location, a format and a scope.
why: Roles are write, hold and blobs: JSONL where git needs it, SQLite where volume does. The index is derived and disposable.

claim: Replication is set union by segment lists.
why: A segment closes once committed, so branches only add files, and a committed segment changing outside an erase is the alarm. A static place is closed segments named by hash plus one mutable segments.json.

claim: A realm is the stores its root name table reaches.
why: Membership is a link, not containment. Across realms: compose by default, bridge only as an explicit signed tick, never replicate. A public store is a standing bridge, declared with presence.

claim: Federation is each person's own store, plus composition.
why: Replies carry the thread's root in about; a ping says only where to look. Admission filters and weight ranks.

claim: A lens is a collector with a base.
why: Render roundtrip requires nonempty, distinct section ids. Put-get additionally requires distinct base ids and the exact same ordered id list in the edit. A public reader refuses a base without distinct ids. A dropped section retains its old body. The broader lens plan records a base of tick, lens hash and audience. It renders, parses edits, diffs by id and emits a changeset. Committed renders are promotions. One tick can have several renders. Absence is never an edit. Anything an observer writes remains its own record.

claim: D1: A public lens refuses a base that repeats a section id.
why: The refusal is base-id-duplicate. The base is checked before the text is read, so the refusal is given whatever the text says. The raw matching keeps its first-match behavior and its distinct-id premise.

claim: Context travels by tick.
why: Proposed context design: references have five states: here, fetchable, withheld, erased or unreachable. Bundles carry what the receiver cannot fetch, filtered by its grant. A session witness tick records known ids and supports key retirement. A brief cites a signed tick record. A cloud run borrows a place and syncs at each tick. These transitions remain future work.

claim: An emit may state a base, and then it names what was live in that base.
why: loops emit names every live record the store holds now. A writer who read earlier, a lens applying an edit or an agent acting on a context it was given, then replaces a setter it never read, and nothing shows it: 2,975 of 10,127 keys in the experiment. Against a stated base, a tick or ids, the same emit leaves a visible conflict instead. With no base an emit claims its writer read everything the store holds. Ruled on 2026-11-20 and built on 2026-11-22 as --base and --base-id; the law is keyed.base. A base that leaves out a record under its own is taken together with what is under it, and the writer is told (ruled on 2026-11-22). Whether a strict store warns or fails on such an emit is left for standing. Version 36.

group: The local API and its surfaces
claim: One API under every surface.
why: Planned API: pure functions and a realm handle that narrows grants, never widens them. Identity-aware reads use fold; tick and witness match the two proposed tick forms. Refusals have closed codes. Future serve JSON-RPC mirrors the crate for LSP, MCP and front ends.

group: The local API and its surfaces
claim: No subscriptions, no coordinator.
why: A watcher owns its checkpoint. Future boundaries run where the handle receives records. Content ticks can run anywhere with matching inputs; witness ticks need their signing key. Boundary and tick transition proofs remain future work.

group: The local API and its surfaces
claim: The CLI is verb first, with the API's verbs.
why: The loops CLI is built for one person (step 2): HTTPie-style payload syntax, JSON answers, no zoom flags. A changeset is written whole or not at all. serve and the API beside it remain proposed.

claim: The limits, in four tiers.
why: Not the model, not in the core, not yet (each with a trigger), outside by design. Something enters the core only if two separate cases need it and it can't be built from records, ticks and lenses. No state-machine framework: each vertex already is one.

claim: Budgets guard failures, not size.
why: Tokens per module, public API snapshots, vocabulary prices, dependency allowlists and inward layering define the budget plan. A budget increase needs a ledger entry citing the core rule.

claim: Model laws and external checks guide Rust; the workspace also has characterization tests.
why: The plan rejected unit tests in favor of proofs, vectors, differential fuzzing and scenarios. The Lean model computes protocol-vector answers; separate theorem files prove the listed laws. External standards supply their own expected data. The rule: do not derive expected answers from the implementation under test.

claim: A law counts only where its boundary establishes its hypotheses.
why: The fold laws held. What failed were the boundaries: a law assumed distinct ids or distinct member names, and nothing guaranteed them. Parsing, writing and settling return types that carry their invariants, as Written does, and the laws take those types. Version 35.

claim: An outside review at each modelling step.
why: A reviewer from another lab gets the code and the docs, never our conclusions. Each finding becomes a vector, a theorem or a narrower claim. Codex found three of our five findings on its own and eight more besides.

claim: The design page is built from the repo.
why: Its sections are HTML and its ledger is these records, in design/rethink/. node design/build.mjs renders the page, CI checks the render, strangeloops.dev serves it unlisted, and the claude.ai artifact is a mirror. .loops/ exists since step 2; the ledger still builds from ledger.json, and ledger-drafts.mjs turns it into drafts for loops emit -. Version 35.

claim: Step 2 is closed: loops emits, reads and folds for one person.
why: Signed records over .loops/, one key, one store. A verb that answers from a store that does not check still answers, and is then refused store-not-clean. Kyle closed the step on 2026-11-20. Ticks are step 4 and come next; standing and sharing follow. Version 36.

claim: Step 4 is closed: a tick written on one machine checks the same on a second.
why: loops tick writes a tick and loops tick --check answers same, differs or cannot check, and exits 0 only for same. A tick can cover a cut, by time or by ids, and a write can state a tick as its base. Kyle closed the step on 2026-11-22. Boundaries, markers and the runner were never in its exit and are not built. Adoption comes next: the old stores imported as a shadow, and reads across several stores. Version 37.

claim: A spec names its stores, and each machine binds the names.
why: A name in a spec's from is bound to a directory by a per-user list, by an optional list kept with a group of stores, or by --store name=dir on the command. The spec and its hash are the same on every machine. A name bound to nothing refuses the whole read (store-unknown), so a missing store is never read as an empty one. A read across stores takes their union first. Ruled on 2026-11-23 (the adoption note); being built. Version 37.

claim: A store describes its kinds in a plain file that refuses nothing.
why: .loops/store.json says, for each kind, its key field, its reference fields, what to show and which states are open and closed. The store refuses nothing until standing. The shorthand emit is strict about what it is given: it finds a thing's name from its key field, and stops before it signs on a key that disagrees, a kind the file does not name, a state in neither list, or a reference field holding anything but a reference of a listed kind. It never repairs or guesses; a batch through emit - is written as given. No read depends on the file: with no flag that names the description, a read's JSON is the same with and without it. Ruled on 2026-11-24 (the kinds and references note); being built. Version 38.

claim: A reference is a field; a mention is what a writer states.
why: A kind's reference fields are described and nothing copies their values into about. A copy would sit in the envelope, where an erasure does not reach, and nothing but the erased payload says where a mention came from. What refers to a thing is read from the fields: loops ls --refers-to asks each declared field as a fold's is does, yes, no or unknown, across kinds and across a group's stores, and states what it read. Ruled on 2026-11-24 (the kinds and references note); being built. Version 38.

claim: An old store is imported as a shadow: one signed record for each old fact.
why: A fact of a kind read by a field is a revision of the thing kind:key, in the order the old store took it in. The old time is occurred, a key made for the import signs, the old observer is a mention and the payload is untouched. A kind the old vertex no longer names is left out unless asked for. A trial on four real stores, 2,912 facts, gave the old tool's reading in every field for every thing held by one store. Ruled on 2026-11-23 (the adoption note); being planned. Version 37.

claim: Only a choice that changes bytes or answers comes to Kyle.
why: A choice that changes a record's bytes or id, a result's bytes or hash, a refusal code, or what a spec answers is his, and is asked with a worked example. Every other implementer choice is written in the changelog and stands unless he objects. What is next, what waits on him and what was built are three documents, ROADMAP.md, DECISIONS.md and CHANGELOG.md, and the Decisions page renders them. Ruled on 2026-11-21. Version 36.

claim: The import writes a reference as kind:key where the old store proves it.
why: Where a field's twin resolves to the thing the field names, the import writes that thing's name; in the six homelab stores field and twin agree in all 13,854 facts. A bare key is written so only in fields the group's map names, with no mention added, and several targets become a list. A kind's key field is never rewritten, and a bare key beside a twin is left as entered. Ruled on 2026-11-24 and deferred the same day: Kyle expects to rebuild stores and pick from the originals, so it is built when a store is picked from by its reference fields, and the homelab is not cut over again (the kinds and references note). Version 38.
